query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A pre‐irradiation thermal annealing treatment that induces controlled grain coarsening (i.e., from a nanocrystalline to an ultrafine‐grained state) can suppress the radiation‐induced Cr/V-rich precipitation in W38Ta36Cr15V11 while retaining its low irradiation hardening, thereby also rendering the material more suitable for bulk fabrication.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced by magnetron sputtering (or similar process) with a high density of grain boundaries that act as sites for segregation and subsequent precipitation under irradiation.
generation.intervention: Apply a moderate thermal annealing treatment at a controlled temperature (within a window that promotes limited grain growth to ultrafine sizes without triggering excessive coarsening or unwanted phase transformations) prior to irradiation and bulk fabrication.
generation.conditions: Anneal the as-deposited nanocrystalline alloy at a temperature controlled to induce limited grain growth (parameters to be determined by controlling time and temperature) so that the grain size increases from the nanocrystalline (<100 nm) regime into the ultrafine-grained regime, then subject the annealed samples to energetic-particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa under fusion-relevant conditions (e.g., high temperature similar to reactor service conditions).
generation.mechanism: Increasing the grain size reduces the overall density of high-energy grain boundaries, which are the preferential sites for segregation and subsequent formation of Cr/V-rich precipitates under irradiation. The ultrafine-grained structure still provides sufficient defect sinks to allow efficient point defect recombination, preserving the low irradiation hardening while mitigating precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under energetic-particle irradiation to ~8 dpa, the thermally annealed (ultrafine-grained) alloy will show a directional reduction in the amount of radiation-induced Cr/V-rich precipitates compared to the as-deposited nanocrystalline alloy, while maintaining negligible irradiation hardening. This enhanced microstructural stability is expected to improve its suitability for fabrication into bulk components.
generation.baseline: The unmodified, nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy which under irradiation tends to develop Cr/V-rich second-phase precipitates (with known negligible irradiation hardening) but whose nanocrystalline state is less amenable to bulk fabrication.
generation.boundary: The irradiation is carried out up to approximately 8 dpa under fusion-relevant energetic-particle bombardment, and the annealing treatment must be optimized to achieve ultrafine (~100–500 nm) grains without inducing other deleterious phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact annealing temperature and time required to reach the optimal ultrafine grain size without adverse side effects remain to be fully determined, and the quantitative extent of precipitation suppression is subject to further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W38Ta36Cr15V11 samples: one set remains in the as-deposited nanocrystalline state and the other is subjected to the proposed moderate thermal annealing treatment to produce an ultrafine-grained structure. Expose both sets to energetic-particle irradiation under identical fusion-relevant conditions up to ~8 dpa. Post-irradiation, perform comparative microstructural characterization and mechanical testing.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify the presence, size, and volume fraction of Cr/V-rich precipitates
Atom probe tomography (APT) for compositional and segregation analysis
Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) for grain size assessment
Nanoindentation to measure hardness and detect any irradiation-induced changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (ultrafine-grained) samples show a similar or higher degree of radiation-induced precipitation or if they exhibit adverse changes in hardness compared to the as-deposited nanocrystalline samples under identical irradiation conditions, then the hypothesis that the annealing treatment suppresses precipitation while maintaining low irradiation hardening is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
